speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, December 13, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the statute law relating to income tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would like to inquire whether it is the Government's intention to proceed with the time allocation motion that was introduced on Friday last after the Question Period this afternoon.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Definitely, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, this opening session of this week is part of the experience of this House in hit-and-run contact with the subject of income tax. Bill C-139 had its origin on that nefarious night of November 12, 1981. Then there was another interlude. There were some letters of clarification. There was an interlude until June 28 last. Then there was a statement, which was no other than a budget message, from the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in the latter part of October when this House resumed its sittings.
In that time we have seen the economy of Canada take a further precipitous drop, much of it, I suggest as a result of that disastrous night of November 12, 1981. Stacking it on, we also saw the effects of the national energy policy. The confidence of business and of individuals in Canada did not just fly out the window; it jetted out the window. We know what followed thereon. The Government said that we were into a world-wide recession. Balderdash! We created most of our own.
The National Energy Program took the most successful part of the Canadian economy, lopped off its head and pierced its bod's with any number of doubled-edged swords. That tattered remains of a government can only be called a disgraceful gang of plunderers of the Canadian economy. Because of the National Energy Program and the subsequent actions taken by the Canadian Government, had they been financiers in the private investment field, the Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources (Mr. Chretien) the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could have been up on charges of manipulating the market and driving down the value of corporate stocks, both foreign controlled and Canadian owned, to the extent that that confidence so needed in the investment market by both Canadians and foreigners was gone.
We are now trying to sweep up some of the debris that was left by the former Minister of Finance. What a disastrous term of office he had. The Government has adopted a time allocation frame of mind. This Bill is 300-odd pages long. It is extremely complex and I am sure that 90 per cent of the Members of the Government do not know what it contains. Yet we will be told that we have to deal with it in a matter of a few days, both on second reading and in Committee of the Whole, because the Government's timetable is in such a shambles.
I should like to refer to the committee report of October 5, 1982, Mr. Speaker. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), shared the Chair for that committee with the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). Usually five of us attended meetings, although sometimes there were only four Members there. Once the attendance actually went up to seven Members but I think that was the highest number that was ever present. I think the chairmen of the committee will agree that it was not really consultation as we examined the budgetary process.
At those sessions in late August and in September we obtained observations from various bodies in Canada. The committee met morning, afternoon and evening in order to accommodate witnesses and hear explanations from officials of the Tax Planning Branch of the Department of Finance. Officials from the Department of National Revenue attended as well, but they were not heard. Those of us who attended the sessions derived a good deal of knowledge about the way officials in the Department of Finance think. To them this was consultation, but to me it was only consultation after the event.
I want to see the budgetary process changed, Mr. Speaker. In over 20 years, on both sides of the House, I have been involved in budgets and it has been a most frustrating experience. When I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue I participated, with my colleague who was then the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, in interdepartmental considerations of income tax changes. That was purely an in-house operation and as Parliamentary Secretaries we had to be exceedingly tough and tell the

officials that certain things they proposed just would not fly. That is not enough, but is not the type of process one wants.
1 will not talk this morning about individual points of detail; 1 would have to speak for two hours and I am allowed only 20 minutes. These points will be coming up in future discussions, in which I intend to participate fully. But we should understand what we are after, and that is, at this time of year, a statement of budgetary intentions wherein the Government generally lays out its program-how much money will be required and what areas of Government revenues are suffering. Then we could have Hon. Members of the House and of the other place, the public, major economic associations, manufacturing groups and individuals make their comment, and some time in October we could settle on the budget and get it through. This would tell people precisely what they may anticipate.
Since November 12, 1981 we have had nothing but a great degree of uncertainty in soft costs and capital cost allowances. The premiums for medical services in private plans were added on to the income of individuals for whom payments were made; the previously very successful income-averaging contracts, the IAACs, were cancelled; and we went into forward averaging. This is all fine for a socialist Government. It is purely a socialist proposition because the money has to be paid by the individual to the Government and then may be claimed back under the plan, whereas, under income-averaging contracts, it went into private investment and represented a great deal of money. We will get to discussing the other deterrents of participating in forward averaging.
No, this is not the way we should proceed with regard to dealing with the budget. We certainly should not have to deal with a collection of all the left over sweepings on the floor, having been discarded by the tax proposals of 1970 following the Carter report. There is much discarded, disreputable Carter tax theory implemented or included in the November 12 budget. Of course, the Minister did not want to understand, his colleagues did not understand what they were doing and Government backbenchers were in some sort of euphoria, not wanting to know. What I charge them with is not wanting to know what is in the budget and what it means to Canada. Only when people come to them, small-businessmen, for instance, who say "You are killing us with the tax on the dividends to small business" does anything happen.
Incidentally, the theory in the tax program branch is that returns on dividends to an owner of a small business are equivalent to an employee's salary from that small business. As far as the individual is concerned, that is his return. But the small businessman has sleepless nights; he has to worry about meeting payrolls. He has high blood pressure as a result of these activities. He has all the worries. The Finance Department grandiloquently says he should only be getting a salary, that his return is equivalent to a salary. What nonsense.
There is a theory in the Finance Department which has been applicable for years. The Government has a right to every dollar earned by an individual because as the Minister responsible for the Status of Women in her startling proposals said the other day, a spouse's allowance is a tax expenditure, a child allowance is a tax expenditure, the personal allowance given to each taxpayer is a tax expenditure and every incentive is a tax expenditure. In other words, the Crown is giving up that money.
What does the word "expenditure" mean but a putting out of money? This is tax money being put out by the Government. That is absolute socialism right to the rotten core of it. All of that money belongs to the Crown. People have shed sweat and worried and have done all those things that are required to earn that money, be it by way of salary or be it by way of initiative and capability-the doers and the movers in this society-and it is not right. God only knows what the Government thinks. It talks about patting the pioneers on the back. It talks about all the things that have been done, that older generations deserve the accolades of the new generations. But that was not done by telling people that they were working for the Government and that the Government, the state, was allowing them to keep a certain proportion of their earnings. What was allowed to be kept? One can go through all of the documentation of the Finance Department and its philosophy, which is that everything a taxpayer, corporate or individual, is allowed to keep is a tax expenditure to be controlled by the Minister of Finance and his minions. That is the philosophy. That is the end result. I will hear the views of the former Parliamentary Secretary, but that is the net result.
We are told that the net result of an increase in child allowance will be increased tax expenditures. We are told that incentives with regard to multiple residences, or MURBs, are tax expenditures. That is nonsense, I believe. I have had a lifetime of exposure to these matters and I find it incomprehensible and an abuse of language for the Government to say that everything that the taxpayer keeps in income tax represents an expenditure by the state. In other words, we all exist for the benefit of the state. That is a total denial-
That is false.

Let the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre show how the operation of the philosophy of income tax under the Liberal administration is other than that.
I see you are getting anxious, Mr. Speaker, and I recognize that I have had my 20 minutes. I hope to raise this subject again in some other guise because this is a matter which must be brought to the attention of the people of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. 1 trust that this will be in the spirit that motivated the committee to provide this exchange and that it will not be statement or diatribe that cannot be answered or that the period will be occupied by others for the whole time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Chair recognizes the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Peterson).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not to ask questions of the Hon. Member for Edmonton West but to respond to some of the charges he has made. I believe I do this in the spirit which he has just articulated in order to suggest to Members of the House the directions that we perhaps should be pursuing in the future with respect to our fiscal policy, monetary policy and the development of our general economic climate in Canada.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton West laced his remarks with hyperbole and misinformation. For example, is it Canada's fault or is this Government to blame for the situation which is taking place in energy throughout the entire world, a world of chaos? Absolutely not. Can he say that the budget of November 12 is responsible for the recession in Canada?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Is it responsible for the recession in the United States, in the entire western industrial world, or the entire world? This type of hyperbole does not help us find the constructive solutions which we have an obligation to find for the people of Canada.
In that spirit, I believe that we on all sides of the House should look at what we can do and suggest for both the short and long-term benefit of Canada's economy. For the short term, I suggest we must provide the support mechanisms which will enable viable businesses to weather our current recession.
Over the longer term, we must set our goals for the productivity of Canadians. By this I mean we must set our goals on becoming world leaders in producing certain products both in our existing industries and in the industries and technologies of the future.
What is the role of a Government in this quest, this pursuit of our short-term and our long-term objectives? There are many roles for the Government to play, but the most important, I believe, is the role involved in creating a favourable monetary and fiscal regulatory environment, a favourable climate in these areas in which the private sector in Canada can thrive to the maximum extent possible.
Dealing with monetary policy first, I believe that individual businesses, big and small, and investors in Canada cannot
Income Tax
survive a tremendous resurgence in interest rates such as we have experienced in the past. It would be incredible today if interest rates were again to skyrocket. What would be our alternatives if interest rates in the United States start to go back up to the unprecedented high which we saw one year ago? We have a number of alternatives available to us and I just want to mention perhaps two. If we were to keep our interest rates lower than those in the United States, naturally foreigners would come here to attempt to borrow on Canada's capital markets. We could protect our capital markets from this type of foreign borrowing which would have the tendency to drive our rates up even higher. We could protect our capital markets, which would then have low interest rates, by resorting to techniques such as the interest equalization tax which was used by the United States for over a decade. This would be one approach we should consider.
Another approach, and I believe it merits the serious consideration of Members of this House, would be to allow a modest or reasonable drop in the exchange value of the Canadian dollar as against the American dollar. This would certainly have some adverse impacts, but I think that on the whole looking at this type of approach might produce some positive benefits for Canadians. I would like to hear discussion on that type of point.
On the monetary side, as well our financial institutions have a very important role to play in both the short term and the long term. Let us consider our banks. In helping the private sector through the current recession, our financial institutions in Canada have an obligation to make available after-tax financing to our small businesses through the Small Business Development Bonds and other programs put in place by our Government.
Oh, oh!
Where did you get the idea, Jim?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
We have created the environment in which these types of instruments can be issued to provide less of a cash drain on businesses in difficulty.
Our financial institutions have an obligation to make small businesses in difficulty aware of these instruments and to cooperate with them in every way possible to see that those who need assistance get that type of financing. That is why we put these measures in place. I am also concerned, with the tremendously huge financing which the banks have given to our bigger companies both in Canada and offshore. With the recession coming on, and with what our finance Committee found out about the banks being highly leveraged, I am concerned that our banks do not try to pull back their lines of credit as they affect small businesses in Canada.
It is much easier, we know, to go to small business people who have been building operations over the years and say to them, "We are calling your lines of credit". Small businesses do not necessarily have the clout of the billion dollar corporations here and abroad. Our financial institutions cannot, if it is

their tendency, pull back those lines of credit from viable small businesses.
Unfortunately, I know of a couple of bad examples. People have come to me whose small businesses, employing 30 to 80 people, have not been adversely affected because of the recession, but even though they have maintained their businesses and have not defaulted on any bank loans, their bankers have come to them and said: "We will pull your loans". That is irresponsible. It creates additional unemployment. It is our small businesses which need that help in these tough times. Banks and financial institutions might be having difficulty with some big loans, but they have an obligation to support our small businesses.
I would also hope that we could get through many of the measures which have been before the House for a long period of time so that we could go on to new types of legislation, such as that dealing with our loan and trust institutions, so that they could enter into commercial lending and become an added source of funds, particularly for small business.
I also believe it would be worthwhile to study the investment powers of our major financial institutions; for example, our insurance companies and our loan and trust institutions. As Hon. Members are aware, they have the power to invest only 8 per cent of their funds in small, unproven enterprises, enterprises which do not have a proven track record. These institutions currently have very little ability to promote venture capital, to go out and help people who have an idea and are prepared to back it with all their managerial and technical ability, to get those new small businesses of the future going. The big institutions do not have the power to get into those areas.
I believe we should consider the possibility of increasing the size of the basket clause of our financial institutions. We might even consider the possibility that, in return for increasing their investment powers, they would have a greater obligation to consider the new types of ventures which the inventive genius of the Canadian entrepreneur is coming up with all the time.
The second area, after monetary policy and the role of our financial institutions, which I believe we must study in order to create a favourable type of economic environment for a recovery is our regulatory environment. The Task Force on Regulatory Reform made numerous recommendations as to the ways by which we can reduce the burden of regulation on the private sector. I am pleased to say that the former President of the Treasury Board and his successor have succeeded in implementing many of those reforms. I am delighted with the commitment of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) to continue on that path and to bring in additional reforms which will increase the consultative process and the opportunity for business, for labour and for environmentalists to participate with the Government in determining what types of regulations would best serve the needs of all Canadians.
Fiscal policy is the third arm of the trio of areas we must study in order to help restore and bring about the type of economic environment we want in Canada. We face a dilemma in this area. Business investors need fiscal certainty. They must
be able to compute their cash flows, their return on investment, for a reasonable period of time. Otherwise, one cannot expect them to make the investment or commitments we need from the private sector. We must ask ourselves, is this need for fiscal certainty, a climate for fiscal stability, incompatible with the concept of tax reform? I do not believe it necessarily is.
The answer, I believe, depends on how one goes about the process of tax reform. First, there are many areas in our Income Tax Act, in our codes, which require rethinking. If we go about rethinking these changes in close consultation with the private sector, in co-operation, where we do it openly and allow much opportunity for input from those who will be affected in the short term and the long term, we will have the ability and knowledge to avoid changes which would upset that climate of fiscal certainty which is a key to economic recovery.
[DOT] >1140)
Secondly, for those who might be affected by reform, we can have generous resort to grandfathering clauses. In other words, we can say: "We are going to change the law, but since you made your investment and business decisions under the former law, you can continue for a reasonable period of time as if the former law under which you made your decisions continues to apply". I believe that type of spirit and co-operation can create the necessary fiscal environment.
What are some of the areas which I believe we, as Members from all sides of the House, should be looking at for reform? One is capital gains. Have we taken a good look at the effect inflation has on capital gains? How much of the gains people experience on their investments are merely inflationary and do not represent real gains? What about the farmers? Should we be reconsidering more realistic valuation dates for farms? What role do farms play in providing the retirement income of people who choose to leave their farms?
I would also like to ask, what about the role of investors and entrepreneurs? If, for example, a business person takes his small savings, say $5,000, and through diligence and entrepreneurial flair builds that operation up into a million dollar company and then wants to sell it, there would be taxes payable in the area possibly of $250,000. We have to ask ourselves, should we leave that $250,000 in the hands of the entrepreneur to reinvest in Canada and create more jobs, or should we leave it in the hands of the Government? Who can best go out and bring about economic recovery by creating new jobs? I believe that one of the things we should reconsider is the possibility of a rollover where an investor reinvests in Canada to create jobs here in Canada.
Another area I think we should look at is tax simplification for small businesses. Some of the most difficult and complicated provisions in the Income Tax Act relate to small businesses.
I do not think that only accountants and lawyers should make money out of these types of provisions.
Research and development is the key to our economic growth in the future. We believe we should take a very expanded view of what research and development involves. There are companies in Canada who do not fall within that traditional concept of research and development. They have

perhaps made design changes to such things as furniture. I know of one furniture company which has come up with new designs, and in spite of the fact that the furniture business is in difficulty in Canada, this one company is selling around the world. Their new designs and new products create new jobs for Canadians.
I think we should, in consultation with the private sector and the Opposition Parties, look at our incentives. Right now, under certain circumstances the private sector pays only 20 per cent of new research and development undertakings and initiatives. That is, in some cases, if they are increasing over the previous couple of years the investments they are making in these areas. Maybe we should get rid of that requirement for incrementality. Let us start talking about this and examining it together.
What about new venture capital for research and development for the new high tech, for the new sunrise industries? We have instruments called scientific research investment contracts which have been the brainchild of the private sector. Maybe we should be creating new types of investment vehicles on a federal basis that individuals can put their money in. There would be a tax conduit principle so that these types of operations can be institutionalized.
We know from the past what we have been able to do in terms of MURBs to help housing and create rental housing for Canadians. We know what we have been able to do with drilling funds in order to spur that type of investment. We know what we have been able to do for films. To me, one of the most important areas is to get this new technology operative and create new jobs. We should be looking at new mechanisms for facilitating that type of investment.
I also believe we have a tremendous opportunity in Canada because of the infrastructure that we have. The service industries that we have in Canada, our financial institutions, our accounting firms, our legal firms, our banks, our insurance institutions; all of these have given us a tremendous advantage when it comes to international competition. Should we not be looking at the possibility of expanding Canada's role as an international financial capital?
We should be looking at provisions in our tax treaties and in our Income Tax Act. This would enable foreigners to seek the stability of the Canadian environment, of the North American climate, to come here with their money, bring their money in, have their investments serviced here, have headquarters here for international operations and have the multinational corporations situate here in Canada using our service industries, using the stability that we have brought in the past to this type of circumstance.
These are just a few of the approaches which 1 believe we should consider on a non-partisan, non-confrontational basis, as Members of this House and in consultation with the private sector, with business and with labour. We are going to get a consensus for economic action in the 1980s by working together, government, business and labour, and I welcome the
Income Tax
breakthroughs that have been made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), particularly in building the bridges of communication to the labour leaders in Canada. He deserves tremendous credit for having done this. He deserves great credit for having responded to the representations made by numerous people in the private sector in the drafting of his mini-budget of last October. This type of consultation, this type of input, this type of co-operation is critical to our future.
I commend the Minister of Finance. It is the path and the process of the future. It is what we need.

speechtext: Just one other question, if I may, Mr. Speaker, on a different matter about which the Parliamentary Secretary spoke. The Parliamentary Secretary will know that the original concept of the Small Business Development Bond was debt consolidation for small business. It has now been changed so that small businesses have to be going broke before they can get a small business development bond, if they can get one. Is that what the Parliamentary Secretary meant when he said the Government created the environment for the Small Business Development Bond?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
The point which the Hon. Member is bringing up is exactly the one which I was making-the necessity for our financial institutions to utilize the Small Business Development Bond and the Small Business Bond to provide help, as a bridging mechanism, for those small businesses which are in difficulty and have to weather the recession. We want them to be whole, to come out of this recession. We want them to maintain their employment levels. We want them to be poised for a "take-off'. This type of approach is critical to helping those small businesses which have cash flow difficulties.
I suggest there is no magical solution that we in Ottawa are going to be able to bring about to do this. We can help try to create the instruments and the climate under which these things can go; but let us face it, it requires the co-operation of our financial institutions which are in the lending business as well.
I called today on the financial institutions, and I hope the Hon. Member for Simcoe North will as well, to work with our small businesses to help them get through this recession, whole and ready and poised to take off in the future.

Mr. Speaker, the November 12 budget created a number of monsters, and now we are removing them two years later. The point raised by the Hon. Member, that the Government had nothing to do with creating or worsening the depression, is very difficult to understand. For instance, the November 12 budget virtually stopped the sale of farm lands in Western Canada because it made it necessary for a person who was selling by instalments to pay the total capital gains on that land before he even received the money. How can the Hon. Member say that the Government's programs did not worsen and deepen the depression in this country?

There is one thing I can assure the House of. The Minister of Finance has been extremely open to good, concrete suggestions as to how we can make our tax system work more productively for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Peterson). I would like to return for just a moment to the issue of Small Business Bonds, and in particular his statement that the Government today is trying to create an atmosphere which will allow the economy to come out of its present recession. I am sure the situation in the Parliamentary Secretary's riding is no different from the situation which I find in Peterborough, and that is that farmers and small businessmen-and I have the letters to substantiate it-cannot obtain Small Business Development Bonds in order to come out of this recession because the banks will not make them available. The Government has the power, does it not, to demand that the banks make these Small Business Development Bonds available to farmers and businessmen who are going out of business at an ever increasing rate? When will the Government act?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on the tax Bill before us today and to stress one theme, and that is that we have a taxation system in Canada which is very unfair, one that generally gives the breaks to the wealthy people, to the big corporations, at the expense of the poor, the ordinary working person, farmers and small business.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the Hon. Member, the usual practice is to refer to Members of the House by constituency, or their function in the case of Cabinet Members.

As I was saying, we have a very unfair taxation system in this country. The Bill before us today will make it even more unfair by loading more and more on the ordinary income person. For example, there is the provision for a partial deindexation, applying the six and five program to indexation in Canada. According to calculations, that will raise $1.7 billion in 1983-84, depending on the inflation rate. The tables I have show that when you partially deindex the taxation system, the lower income person pays more than his or her fair share. The wealthier person will get off much easier.
Let us take the example of a single person earning $7,500 a year. When you partially deindex the taxation system to take into account the six and five program, that person will pay an extra $113 in income tax in 1984, which means a tax increase for that person of 15.7 per cent. The person earning $10,000 will pay an extra $119, for an increase of 14.7 per cent. The person earning $50,000 will pay an extra $591, which is an

January 31, 1983
Income Tax
increase of only 4.1 per cent in that person's income tax. A person earning over $100,000 will have an increase in percentage terms of only 2.5 per cent. Is that just and fair? I maintain that it is not. We need a taxation system in this country based on the ability to pay. As the Bishops pointed out, those who earn the least, the 20 per cent at the bottom, earn only 4 per cent of the national income. They should get hit less hard than those earning $50,000, $60,000, $70,000 or $100,000 a year.
The same applies to the married taxpayer. A taxpayer earning $20,000 a year, with two dependants under the age of 18, with partial deindexation will have to pay an extra $254, an increase of 21.7 per cent. A wealthy person making over $100,000 a year, with the same two dependants, will have an increase of 3.2 per cent. I maintain, and suggest to the Government and this House, that it should be the opposite way. Someone making over $50,000 or $100,000 a year should pay even more income tax. Someone earning under $30,000, $20,000 or $15,000 should pay less income tax. That is the only way if we want a fair taxation system, one that is based on compassion, reason and ability to pay. That has not been the case in this country under Liberal and Conservative Governments for the past 100 years.
Let us look at the corporate tax rate. A few minutes ago we heard from the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). He shed a lot of crocodile tears because of companies that are paying so much in taxes. He said that because they paid so much tax, they will not expand and they will not invest. He asked what this would do to the job situation and so on. If you look at the record, Mr. Speaker, you find that corporations in Canada have paid less and less in taxes over the last five or six decades while the individual has had to pay more in taxes. I maintain that is not fair.
Let us look at the statistics. In 1952, 53.7 per cent of federal Government revenue came from corporations and 43.6 per cent from individuals. In 1962, ten years later, 40.1 per cent comes from corporations and 59.9 per cent from individuals. In 1980, just a couple of years ago, 30.5 per cent came from corporations and 69.4 per cent came from individuals.
The share of taxes paid by ordinary citizens in this country has increased from 46 per cent in 1952 to 69.4 per cent in 1980, while the share paid by corporations went down from 53.7 per cent in 1952 to 30.5 per cent in 1980.
I suggest that the priorities of this Government are the wrong ones. Instead of trying to redistribute the tax load in Canada in a more fair, equal and compassionate direction, the Government has redistributed the tax load in the opposite way by bringing in all kinds of incentives, tax cuts, tax credits and tax loopholes for the very wealthy and the corporations in this country. Time and again it has loaded it on to the ordinary citizen.
It strikes me as strange that whenever the country is in trouble, the solution is to give more incentives to the rich so that they will do better, and the solution for the poor is to tighten their belts so that they will do better. That is not fair. It is not the kind of Canada that I, and I suspect the majority of Canadians, want.
It is not only the federal Government; we must take into consideration the provincial Governments as well. When we look at their taxation system, such as unemployment insurance contributions and so on, we find the same trend developing. In terms of federal and provincial revenues, in 1950 corporations paid 49.2 per cent. In 1980, corporations carried 23.3 per cent of the national tax load. In 1950, individuals paid 50.7 per cent; in 1980, their share had risen to 76.6 per cent. That is neither fair nor just. The principal thing that we in this House should be doing is to change that kind of tax system, bringing in many of the recommendations made in this country over the years for a more fair and just tax system.
If we change the tax system so that the poor, the ordinary worker, the farmer and the small-businessman have more income, they will spend it. They will buy consumer goods. They would buy the necessities of life in order to look after their families. In the process, this would create jobs. We must stimulate consumer spending in this country. We need a tax cut, not for the large companies, but for the ordinary citizen. Large companies have never in the past responded to that kind of incentive and never will. We must get rid of a tax system which is a system of socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor. It is socialism for the rich because, year in, year out, Governments in Canada have given millions and millions of dollars to large companies. In fact, if we had taken equity in the CPR every time we gave it millions of dollars to upgrade rail lines, improve facilities and purchase hopper cars, we would own and control it now. The same is true of many other corporations in the country. We do not give that kind of assistance to ordinary people. We do not give that kind of assistance to the single mother, the unemployed, or the small-businessman or small farmer unfortunate enough to go bankrupt. That is the kind of thing we want to change.
In 1982 the budget levied a corporate surtax of 5 per cent which will be reduced in 1983 to 2.5 per cent. That perpetrates the kind of unfairness and lack of compassion that the country shows for the ordinary citizen.
On the other hand, only about .07 per cent of our GNP is in the form of a wealth tax. In the United States, about .42 per cent of the GNP is taken up by wealth tax, while in Switzerland 1.02 per cent goes to wealth tax. If we want to base our taxation system on fairness, then I suggest we examine what other countries are doing to help the ordinary citizen. But so far that has not been done.
Another point I want to raise has been referred to by the Parliamentary Secretary, and that is whether the valuation day for farmers should be changed. In 1980 the Liberal Party promised that it would be. I am sure Hon. Members opposite recall that they were to change valuation day from December 31, 1971 to December 31, 1974 and that it was to be indexed so that there would be a more appropriate reflection of the inflation in land prices. Nearly three years have passed and that promise has not been fulfilled. 1 do not think it is a question of whether it should be fulfilled. The Government
January 31, 1983

made a commitment and it must deliver. This is very important because land prices are being inflated day in and day out. If the valuation day is not changed and some form of indexation adopted, then small and middle-sized farmers will be paying the largest increase in taxes, in this case through capital gains.
Those are a few of the points that should be made, Mr. Speaker. In Canada we have a taxation system that is extremely unfair and regressive and which loads taxes on the ordinary citizen, the ordinary worker, the farmers and the poor in the country. They pay all kinds of consumer taxes and sales taxes which are regressive. At the same time, we allow the wealthy all kinds of incentives and investment tax credits and allow large corporations to pay less than their fair share. That is not the kind of Canada I want. I want a Canada based on freedom for the individual to do his utmost. That cannot happen while he is saddled with extremely high taxes.
We have an immense deficit and I am afraid that, as it increases, the ordinary person will have to pay the price, through increased taxes and programs like six and five which will hit him the hardest. The six and five program is a good example of what happens. If someone is making $10,000 per year and is limited to a 5 per cent increase, that amounts to $500. But if someone is making $50,000 per year the increase is $2,500. Where is the equity in a program which was supported by the federal Liberal and Conservative Parties? There is no equity in it, Mr. Speaker, but I suggest that neither Party is willing to stand up for the ordinary citizen or to represent him in this House. We should be making some real changes to benefit the ordinary citizen, rather than throwing more and more to the big companies and the wealthy people in the country.

I believe that foreign ownership in general has made this country poor and has cost many, many jobs. Government
Income Tax
statistics show that foreign companies import four times as much as Canadian firms. Foreign ownership has prevented us from having a rational and planned industrial system. It has fragmented the industrial base that we do have and has allowed a good deal of R and D to go south of the border and into other countries.
We are the only industrialized country in the world that has allowed so much foreign ownership and I think the time has come when that should end. It can be ended in the oil industry by making sure that Petro-Canada expands.

Mr. Speaker, first I want to pay tribute to the Members of Parliament who joined with me during the month of September and sat on the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to listen to businessmen, construction people and professionals from across Canada make proposals that would lay the groundwork for, and give us insight into, the changes required in order to come up with a more equitable tax system. I am referring particularly to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher), and the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who certainly had a tremendous input into the Committee and was a very active participant on a regular basis.
I was somewhat disappointed. I hoped perhaps there could have been more regular attendance before that Committee because the calibre of submissions was extremely good and each was backed up by a level of common sense which made it easily understood by all involved. I could not help but be somewhat alarmed by the lack of knowledge of the Small Business Bond. Under the Small Business Bond Program banks do not pay income tax on interest earned. If they are in a non-profit situation-and their profits have been dropping badly because of the recession in the western world for the last several months-naturally they will not have as much profit to invest as they had, for example, a year ago when many bonds were negotiated between the borrower and the lender. I know there is a great need for this, but in fact they are not in a taxable position. We as a Government cannot force them to make loans even if they are in a taxable position because it has to be negotiated, I say again, between the borrower and the lender.
Also I should like to comment briefly on some of the submissions that were made. Some of them pointed out to all members of the Committee that there were sectors of the economy where perhaps the capital cost allowance factor needed adjustment due to the short life period of the particular equipment purchased. I am talking here about submissions that were made and the cross-examination of the persons from the Canadian Construction Association.
Also I should like to touch upon the issue raised by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) concerning the application of the capital gains tax. This is another issue which was raised within Committee. I believe it was the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which made the proposal that perhaps one of the most equitable ways of applying a tax in that
Income Tax
particular area would be to tie it to the length of tenure or the length of ownership.
I sympathize with the situation the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville has described of a farming operation on which perhaps a farmer or his family have worked for several generations to build up an equitable and viable operation, only to be faced with a system of taxation that in the last few years, during an inflationary spiral, has made it very difficult to cope with the transfer or sale of that property. In one sense, perhaps it has slowed down the takeover of Canadian land by foreign owners. But in the other context we have to be very careful that we do not destroy the family farm concept.
I would like to see consideration given not only to the suggestion made by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce but also to an alternative system of indexing in this same situation. Indexing has already been accepted by our country. We index our personal income tax base, our pensions and various other aspects of our economy that affect people's lives. This may be a good time to look at this.
If we look back over the last several months, in particular the four months prior to December 1, the rate of inflation on a monthly basis has been running at approximately one-half of 1 per cent. In contrast to the way the inflationary impact is calculated in the United States, we calculate ours on the 12-month moving average. Consequently, if we consider inflation in the four months prior to December 1 to be at a rate of approximately one-half of 1 per cent, then we realize that Canada's inflation rate has been running at 6 per cent during that time, and there was negative inflation during the month of December, then we have achieved our purpose as far as the inflationary spiral is concerned, although it may not appear that way when one looks at the 12-month moving average and compares it to the monthly averages in the United States.
However, there is another area that perhaps we should examine very closely. Canadians are great savers. In the year 1981 I believe Canadians salted away something like $17 billion in savings as far as private investors are concerned. This money is badly needed in the small business and farming sectors.
Another possible vehicle to examine is that of finding another way to channel some of these savings back into the investment sector, particularly into those areas where it is so badly needed. Perhaps this could be examined in committee. Maybe we can come up with a vehicle that would ensure security to the investor and stability to the owner. I believe this can be done. I speak as a private Member of the House of Commons when I make this suggestion.
You can't; you are a Parliamentary Secretary.

I believe this suggestion would give us a boost in the arm. We have resources in Canada which are not available in other countries in the world. We are the second
January 31, 1983

Income Tax
largest country in the world as far as geographical area is concerned. This huge diversity in our economy spread over such a large country has made it very difficult to apply a tax system that is completely equitable to everyone.
It is in this context that I am most appreciative of the way organizations submitted briefs to us during the month of September. There were those of us who did not take any holidays but stayed to work to ensure that the proposals coming from the business community could be closely examined in committee and the appropriate suggestions sent on for consideration for the upcoming budget later this year.
I mentioned earlier briefs were submitted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Construction Association. We also had briefs from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Professional Accountants. All of these organizations had something to contribute.
One of the problems we have as a governing body, and I speak in this context for all Members of the House of Commons, is the diversity of our economy here in Canada. We have to work toward a solution that is fair and applicable to all of Canada. After the committee ended its work and Parliament resumed sitting, we had a submission by the Canadian Federation of Retail Farm Equipment Dealers in Canada, who asked for consideration of the proposal that the investment tax credit be applied to used equipment. This was an area which the dealers found was creating problems for them. They were carrying huge inventories of farm equipment which were not moving because of the investment tax credit on new equipment as well as the half-year depreciation allowance, and coming toward the end of the year it is to a person's benefit to buy new equipment instead of used equipment.
With all of the input we have had to date and the adjustments made in the budget papers, I think it accurately reflects the requirements that will be in place as our economy starts to turn and we achieve the level of stability required in the small business, agricultural sectors and other sectors that contribute to the welfare of this nation.
I was interested to note that, as of November 20, there were more oil wells drilled and completed in Canada from January 1, 1982 to November 20, 1982 than there had been in any other year since 1977, with the sole exception of 1980. That is an indication that the oil and energy sector has started to turn.
I see some puzzled looks on the other side of the chamber, but bear in mind that I said oil wells drilled and completed, not oil and gas wells. I see an Hon. Member looking at me curiously, but I would have to ask him why drill another gas well when we have so many drilled and capped for which markets are not available? I notice that the National Energy Board has provided permits to increase our exports that I hope will bring those capped wells back into production and give some new life to the economy in that sector.
It is also interesting to note that the plans announced toward further development, not only in the Arctic and the Beaufort but in the offshore, show that very large companies have faith
in our Canadian tax system and are willing to make those kinds of expenditures that will create additional jobs and bring our economy back to the level of prosperity that we had a few years ago before the world recession set in.
In spite of the fact that we in Canada think we are very hard pressed-indeed we are; our unemployment figure is far higher than we would like to see it-when we compare our situation to other industrialized nations in the western world, we do have the basic human and natural resources that should allow us to take advantage of the quick recovery that we hope will start this coming summer.
In closing, I want to point out that we have made a tremendous number of changes to the Income Tax Act. I believe these changes are well spread out and cover a wide range of concerns, from the automobile standby charges to the liabilities of directors of corporations, withholding tax and so on. These changes have been brought about as a result of the Government consulting with concerned individuals as well as from the representations made to the committee by the people of Canada when it sat in the month of September.
We hope that consideration will be given in the budget later this year to some long-term proposals which will have to be implemented over the next few years in order to meet the needs of a changing society and a changing business world.

speechtext: The period of question and answer having now expired, the Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon).

Mr. Speaker, while the frustrations of these question sessions are most felt by the Hon. Member next expected to speak, 1 must say that I believe these exchanges are very valuable to the House and to the people of Canada. In particular, they reveal the difficult dilemma of Members of Government in being faced with questions which the Canadian people have been asking with regard to the November 12 budget for more than a year. The answers appear to be the same today as the Government has been giving all along.
When we asked about the impact of reducing first year depreciation by 50 per cent on an item which is on the fast depreciation rate of three or five years, for example, it was impossible for Government Members to argue against the fact that this measure of the budget of November 12, 1981, included in Bill C-139 before us, does not destroy jobs. In fact, some 20 per cent of the automobiles manufactured in Canada are purchased for lease or rental and are normally written off over three years. Suddenly, the operating costs of a lease or rental equipment business have been increased by imposing this change. Therefore, the turnover rate of these vehicles is slower and the output from our Canadian automobile and equipment manufacturing industry is reduced. That means the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs.
Therefore, I am very pleased that we are giving Government Members, backbenchers in particular, an opportunity to reveal some of the hypocrisy in the position the Government has taken under the leadership of, first, the former Minister of Finance, who introduced the budget over a year ago, and now, more recently, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who has had to jump through hoops and try to justify the introduction of Bill C-139 at such a belated stage of this process.
This particular budget has now been changed 47 times. The Liberal Government has had to retreat from many of the measures and the basic principle on which it was predicated. In fact, it is no longer anything like the budget first introduced on November 12 of 1981. Nonetheless, the major and damaging elements of the budget have largely been retained. This is why members of this Party in particular do not intend to see this budget measure, the Ways and Means motions, go through the House in great haste.
I, for one, resent the implication given in a letter sent out by the Minister responsible for Revenue Canada to my constituency office suggesting that we tell taxpayers that they should urge their Members of Parliament to get this Bill through expeditiously, otherwise they will not be receiving their tax rebates in a timely fashion. I think that is a form of intimidation and blackmail which is absolutely unacceptable to Members of the House.
As we well know, the Government has already been busily collecting tax in accordance with the provisions of the budget of a year ago for a full year. In terms of the tax year ending April 30, 1982, those measures were implemented without the support of legislation or the consent of this House. Now the Government intends to tax in the present taxation period, applying the rules which we again have not adopted as law. Nonetheless, the Minister of Finance has the gall to tell Canadian taxpayers that if Members of Parliament do not get this Bill through the House quickly, then their tax rebates will not be received by April 30, or perhaps not received at all.
That is a fact.

That is the double standard which the Government regularly applies. If the Government takes, it takes without the benefit of the law. If it is required to give back, it also disregards its moral obligation to do so and then tries to accuse Opposition Members of being the problem.
Followed your leadership.

It is important that we very carefully study the provisions of this enabling legislation, Bill C-139. It is very interesting that, in fact, the Canadian Tax Foundation is due to start work on the major issue of restructuring Canada's taxation system. Therefore, one must ask the question, given all of the blunders and retractions of the measures of the original budget, why we are now in such a big rush to implement some of the remaining features which are so damaging to the Canadian economy?
When people in the New Democratic Party and Members of Government say, "We are only trying to be fairer to the ordinary Canadian and extract more revenue from corporations and the wealthy", they do not realize that many of those large corporations have declared a 50 per cent reduction of profits in the past year, that that has a direct relationship to the hundreds of thousands of people they have been laying off, that many of the small businesses and individuals of Canada have declared bankruptcy, personal and corporate, at a rate which is 50 per cent larger than it was in 1980, and that this all translates into the loss of employment.
Therefore, although we argue that our economy is in rough shape because of world oil prices and other factors, Members on the Government benches opposite evade the truth. The truth of the matter is that the November 12 budget was the trigger for a colossal decline in the Canadian economy. The Government now has no right to blame the Opposition for delaying this Bill when we feel the measures contained within it have been the trigger for the economic catastrophe that is unfolding in our country.
On November 12, 1981 the Government projected $66 billion of revenue. The projection of October 28 of last year was $55 billion. In other words, the Government's revenue predictions have dropped by $ 11 billion in one year. At the same time, because of additional unemployment and job program costs, we have seen the financial outlay increase substantially. The budget of November 12, 1981, which was
January 31, 1983

supposedly to raise $9 billion of additional revenue from Canadians over the previous year, has in fact destroyed the revenue base of the Government of Canada.
That confirms a theory that we on this side have discussed in the House several times. In an academic sense, it is called the "Laffer hypothesis", but for ordinary-minded people, this theory merely says that if one continues to raise corporate and personal taxes without limit, one will pass a point beyond which one will reduce the total revenue flow to Government. This theory, this down-to-earth, practical fact, is at the heart of our present economic dilemma. The Government has passed over the peak on what is called the "Laffer curve", and we are now taxing businesses and corporations to the extent that it is no longer worth being in business. That is why the revenues of the Government of Canada have fallen $11 billion over the last year and expenses have increased some $11 billion, so that, for the financial year 1982-83, we will see a total deficit approaching $30 billion. This confirms the theory that Government cannot continue to tax and increase tax without limit.
I read that when the Minister of Finance introduced this Bill shortly before Christmas, he said: "Canadians, as a whole, understand that their Government cannot continue to spend more and more while it taxes them less and less", the implication being that the Government had to raise taxes to pay for spending. Of course, the true nature of the problem is that the Government is spending far too much and doing little about reducing the extravagance and waste for which it is responsible. It is not taxation which is in dispute so much as the lack of fiscal restraint.
I think that if we merely consider the recent Auditor General's report-may I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with considerable astonishment and consternation, Canadians this weekend witnessed the final moments and tragic end of the political career of a party leader. A political organization which claims that it alone has the God-given qualifications for leading the destinies of Canadians, has chosen at a time when it is fifteen points ahead in the public opinion rolls, to sacrifice in fact to literally assassinate its leader.
After sailing in troubled waters for the last two years and after weathering the storm, so to speak, now that better days are on the horizon, the captain is being asked to leave the helm just when he is about to deliver his cargo.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER-PROPOSED ACTION BY PROVINCE OF ONTARIO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have seen the same reports on which I gather the Hon. Member is basing his question. They puzzle me a little bit. There are negotiations under way which are taking place within the context of a court ordered process in the United States. Those are negotiations between the United States Government and the company in the United States. We are in touch with the American Government on those negotiations. We are pressing on them concerns which we would wish to have the company take into account, in the hope that the company and the United States Government will reach the proper safeguards in a proper negotiation.
There is not a negotiation between the Canadian and American Governments, as the newspaper seemed to imply. There is a process of communication and consultation.
I have no objection whatsoever to the provincial Government entering the court process. My only concern, when they undertake that kind of activity, is that they make sure they touch base with other people who are concerned, to ensure that the action is one that will be useful. I hope in this case that they will be concerned not simply with whether their action might affect the federal Government's interest, but that they will make sure that they are in touch with the public interest groups, the pressure groups in the Niagara area who may endorse an intervention by the Ontario Government or have some concerns about it. The answer I am giving him is that there is over $2 billion of stimulus resulting from the budget of my predecessor last June and my economic statement of October 27. That stimulus of over $2 billion is being injected into the economy at the present time. In all my consultations across the country I have received one clear message, that the private sector wanted certainty and stability, and that it wanted this legislation to be implemented without further delay. Madam Speaker, I agree. It makes a lot of sense to inject additional funds into the Canadian economy at the present time. In fact, that is what the Government is doing.
